newsitem.title: NEPAL: India, Nepal vow to strengthen border controls.
newsitem.headline: India, Nepal vow to strengthen border controls.

text.p: Nepal and India pledged on Saturday to strengthen controls over illegal activities across their porous sub-Himalayan border, officials said.

They said a bilateral group on border management recommended greater technical cooperation between the neighbours' law enforcement agencies to check smuggling, terrorism, trafficking in arms and drugs and the sale of young women into prostitution.
"The existing system is not fully effective and it should be strengthened," Karna Dhoj Adhikary, leader of the Nepali delegation, told reporters after the talks.

The panel decided to set up sub-groups to discuss specific issues in detail, including the movement of criminals and illicit goods across the border. The group also agreed to improve communication among border district authorities.
Nepal and India share a 1,500-km (950-mile) border which is open for free movement of their citizens under a 47-year-old treaty between the two South Asian neighbours.
At present, anyone speaking either Nepali or any Indian language or with the physical appearance of a Nepali or Indian national is allowed to move freely across the border.
"There are problems which should be considered in an innovative way," Adhikary said.
India and Nepal pledged in June not to allow their territories to be used for activities directed against the other during a visit to Kathmandu by Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral.
Voluntary organisations say thousands of young Nepali girls are brought across the border every year and sold for as little as $4 to brothels in Bombay, India's commercial capital.
New Delhi says separatist activities of Kashmiri rebels are increasing in Nepal, where sophisticated plastic explosives bound for India were seized earlier this year.

Dozens of guerrilla groups have been waging a separatist revolt in the troubled Himalayan region of Kashmir since 1990. Police and hospitals say more than 20,000 people have died in insurgency-related violence.
Three people suspected of killing a Japanese Buddhist monk in Nepal's Lumbini town, the birth place of Lord Buddha, were arrested this week in New Delhi.
